hints: Focus on what actually happens when chlorine dissolves, it does not just stay as dissolved $\text{Cl}_2$.
Remember chlorine in water undergoes disproportionation to form $\text{HCl}$ and chloric(I) acid, $\text{HClO}$.
Think about which of the listed ions comes from the weak acid $\text{HClO}$ and acts as the powerful oxidising disinfectant.
walkthrough:
**Write what happens when chlorine meets water**

Chlorine does not stay unchanged in water. It reacts in a disproportionation reaction where one chlorine atom is oxidised and the other is reduced.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{Cl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{HCl} + \text{HClO}$$

**Look at the two acid products**

$\text{HCl}$ is a strong acid and fully ionises to $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$. $\text{HClO}$, chloric(I) acid, is a weak acid and sets up this equilibrium.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{HClO} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{ClO}^-$$

**Pick out the disinfectant**

The $\text{Cl}^-$ ion is just a stable spectator ion with no killing power. The species derived from $\text{HClO}$, the chlorate(I) or hypochlorite ion $\text{ClO}^-$, is a strong oxidising agent that kills bacteria and is the active disinfectant.

options.A: Incorrect. $\text{ClO}_2^-$ is the chlorite ion. It is not produced by the reaction of $\text{Cl}_2$ with water, so it cannot be the disinfectant here.
options.B: Incorrect. $\text{Cl}^-$ is the chloride ion from $\text{HCl}$. It is very stable and has no oxidising or disinfecting action, it is just a spectator.
options.C: Incorrect. $\text{HCl}$ is a strong acid that simply gives $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$. Acidity alone is not what disinfects the water in this treatment.
options.D: Correct. $\text{ClO}^-$ is the chlorate(I) ion, also called hypochlorite. It comes from $\text{HClO}$ and is a powerful oxidiser that destroys bacteria, so it is the active killing species.
